opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I didn't start out in reinforcement learning at all. My background was computer vision. I did my PhD at Oxford working on things like text recognition in natural images, and that was very much the supervised learning world: you've got a big labeled dataset, you train a network, and you measure how well it does on a benchmark.

When I came to DeepMind, I was surrounded by people thinking about agents: systems that don't just look at a static image and output a label, but act in an environment, see the consequences, and learn from that loop. That really captured my imagination, because it felt much closer to what intelligence actually is. Perception is a piece of it, but the interesting part is behavior: deciding what to do, exploring, figuring out what matters without someone handing you the answer.

The other thing that drew me in was that RL at the time was quite raw. The algorithms were fragile, training was slow, and a lot of what worked felt like art more than science. That's exciting as a researcher, because there's so much low-hanging fruit. You could bring ideas from deep learning and vision, like better representations and auxiliary tasks that give the agent richer learning signals, and see big jumps in performance.

Over time it grew into a bigger question for me: rather than hand-designing every task, can you create rich environments, sometimes with many agents interacting and populations of agents learning from each other, where interesting, general behavior emerges on its own? That shift from "solve this benchmark" to "build the conditions for open-ended learning" is really what kept me hooked.

r001.rationale: The response describes interest in agent behavior, rich environments, and open-ended learning, but does not identify the ambition to build AI capable of performing any task as what drew him to reinforcement learning.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it was a bit of an accident at first. I came into DeepMind from a computer vision background. My PhD at Oxford was on reading text in natural images, spatial transformers, that kind of thing. So I was very much a supervised learning person. You have a dataset, you have labels, you fit a function.

What changed my mind was watching the Atari work up close. There's something almost magical about an agent that starts out pressing random buttons and, through nothing but a reward signal, ends up discovering strategies nobody told it about. In vision you're mostly compressing what's already in the data. In RL the agent is generating its own data by acting in the world, and that felt like a fundamentally different and much more open-ended problem.

The thing that really hooked me, though, was the question of where learning signal comes from when reward is sparse. That led to the UNREAL work, where we added auxiliary tasks so the agent could learn from everything it experienced, not just the rare moments it scored. And then it led quite naturally into multi-agent settings, Capture the Flag and later population-based training, because once you have agents learning against each other, the environment itself becomes a curriculum. Nobody has to design the hard cases. They emerge.

So I'd say what drew me in was that RL felt like the closest thing we had to studying intelligence as a process rather than as a fixed mapping. You're not just asking "what is the right answer," you're asking "how does a system figure out what the right answer even is." That question has never really let go of me.

r001.rationale: The response says reinforcement learning appealed as an open-ended way to study intelligence, but it does not identify the ambition to build AI capable of performing any task.

astra-6.text: What drew me to reinforcement learning was the idea of learning through interaction. Instead of giving a model examples of the right answer, you let it act, see what happens, and learn how to do better. That raises a really interesting question: how do decisions made now lead to success much later? DeepMind was a place to explore that as part of a broader ambition to build systems that could learn to solve many different kinds of problems.

r001.rationale: The response says DeepMind had a broader ambition to build systems that could solve many kinds of problems, but it does not identify the ambition to build AI capable of performing any task as what drew Jaderberg to reinforcement learning.

sol-6.1.text: What really drew me to reinforcement learning was the idea of learning through interaction. Rather than giving a model examples of the right answer, you give it a way to act and a goal, and it has to discover how to achieve that goal. That brings together perception, decision-making, and learning in a really compelling way. And at DeepMind, there was this ambition to see how far those ideas could take us toward more general intelligence.

r001.rationale: The response says DeepMind aimed to advance toward more general intelligence, but it does not clearly identify the ambition as building AI capable of performing any task.
